heroLead: Rapid City sits about as deep in Antrim Shale country as Michigan gets, and that means most of the wells around here have been producing a long time.
intro: Rapid City isn't a big place, and most of the mineral owners we talk to out here inherited a piece of ground from a grandparent or great-uncle who never drilled a thing themselves — the lease and the well came later, courtesy of whoever owned the Antrim rights underneath. If that's you, you already know the check that shows up every month has gotten smaller over the years. That's not a mistake on the operator's part. That's just what shallow biogenic gas does.

We buy mineral and royalty interests around Rapid City in eastern Kalkaska County. No pressure, no mailbox lowball, no 48-hour deadline. We tell you what the math actually says about your interest and let you decide.

sections.heading: What's Actually Under Rapid City
paragraphs: This end of Kalkaska County sits inside the Antrim Shale core — the Devonian black shale that made northern Michigan a gas play in the 1980s and '90s. It's shallow, usually somewhere between 500 and 2,000 feet, and it's biogenic gas, meaning bacteria did the work over geologic time rather than heat and pressure cooking oil into gas the way it happens in West Texas. That matters for one big reason: Antrim wells come on producing a decent stream of gas and water, then decline hard and fast in the first few years before settling into a long, low, flat tail that can run for decades.

If your well was drilled in the late '80s or '90s boom, it's probably sitting on that flat tail right now. Small checks, but steady ones — and that steadiness is worth something to a buyer even when the monthly number looks unimpressive on paper.

sections.heading: Why Your Royalty Check Doesn't Match What Grandpa Got
paragraphs: We hear this complaint constantly around Kalkaska County: the well used to pay a lot more. It did. Antrim decline curves are steep up front and that's not the operator shorting you — it's the physics of a shallow biogenic reservoir depleting. What's left now is late-life production, and late-life production gets valued differently than a fresh well. A buyer looking at your interest isn't pricing it off what the well made in 1994. They're pricing it off what's realistic for the next 10 to 20 years, discounted back to today.

That's why we won't quote you a number without pulling your actual check stubs or division order first. Anyone who throws out a per-acre price on a Rapid City parcel sight unseen is guessing, and guesses run in whatever direction gets you to sign.

sections.heading: Split Estate and Old Family Deeds
paragraphs: A lot of the mineral ownership out here traces back to farm and timber deeds from decades ago where the surface got sold off separate from the minerals — classic split estate. Kalkaska County's register of deeds has the paper trail, but tracking a fractional interest back through two or three generations of heirs can take real digging, especially if nobody probated an estate properly along the way.

If your name isn't cleanly on the division order, or you're one of six siblings splitting an interest their dad never formally transferred, that's common up here and it's fixable — it just has to get handled before any sale closes, and we'll tell you straight if that's the holdup.

faqs.question: Is my Rapid City interest still worth anything if the well is old?
faqs.answer: Usually yes. Antrim wells with a long flat production tail still have value — it's just priced off the remaining stream, not the boom-year numbers. We look at your actual production history before saying anything about value.

faqs.question: Do you buy small fractional interests?
faqs.answer: Yes. A lot of Kalkaska County ownership got divided across heirs over the years, and a 1/32nd interest is still an interest we'll look at.

faqs.question: What paperwork do you need first?
faqs.answer: A recent check stub or division order gets us started. If you've got an old lease or deed, that helps too, but it's not required for a first look.
